about.title: Downey Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Downey's economy runs on warehousing, logistics, manufacturing, healthcare and retail — industries where lifting injuries, falls, machinery accidents and repetitive-strain harm are common. If you were hurt on the job, California's workers' compensation system should cover medical care and a portion of lost wages regardless of fault. But comp isn't always the whole story: when a negligent third party — a subcontractor, a property owner, an equipment maker, or another driver during a work trip — caused your injury, you may also have a separate claim for the full range of damages comp doesn't pay. LawProactive connects injured Downey workers, at no cost, with an attorney who can sort out both. There's no fee unless your case recovers compensation.
commonInjuries: Falls from ladders, scaffolding or wet floors

whyChoose.title: Comp isn't always the whole claim

items.title: Report the injury promptly
items.desc: California generally requires notifying your employer within 30 days to protect your workers' comp rights. The sooner it's documented, the harder it is to dispute.

items.title: Look for a third-party claim
items.desc: If someone other than your employer caused the injury, you may have a separate case for pain, suffering and full lost earnings — damages workers' comp does not provide.

items.title: Retaliation is illegal
items.desc: It's against California law for an employer to punish you for filing a legitimate work-injury claim. An attorney can protect you if that happens.

items.question: Can I sue my employer for a Downey workplace injury?
items.answer: Usually workers' compensation is your exclusive remedy against your employer, regardless of fault. But if a third party — like a contractor, property owner or equipment manufacturer — caused your injury, you may be able to bring a separate personal injury claim against them.

items.question: What if my workers' comp claim is denied?
items.answer: A denial is not the end. You can appeal, and an attorney can help gather medical evidence and represent you in the process. Many valid claims are initially denied.

items.question: How long do I have to act?
items.answer: Report the injury to your employer as soon as possible (generally within 30 days), and be aware that third-party injury claims carry their own two-year California deadline. Talking to an attorney early keeps every option open.
